audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Does the P2P gossip validation layer validate commitment_indices bounds before passing to verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl?

phase1.summary: The 'commitment_indices' in this codebase are column indices (sidecar.Index, uint64, 0-127 for 128 columns), not array indices into the commitments slice. The Go layer in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs populates the 'indices' slice with sidecar.Index for each row-element pair. The upstream VerifyDataColumnSidecar (p2p_interface.go:37) enforces sidecar.Index < numberOfColumns before the KZG path is reached. The c-kzg-4844 binding validates equal array lengths before C is called. No out-of-bounds array access pattern exists in the Go layer.
state_anomalies: The semantic meaning of 'commitment_indices' in the property description does not match the code: these are column indices (0-127), not indices into the commitment array.
VerifyDataColumnSidecar validates sidecar.Index < numberOfColumns (line 37) via ValidFields() which is called before validateWithKzgBatchVerifier. This check is correct and runs first.

The C library receives cellIndices as column identifiers, not as array offsets. Out-of-bounds cell_index (e.g., cellIndex >= CellsPerExtBlob=128) would cause C_KZG_BADARGS from the C library, returned as an error (not a panic).
phase1.concurrency_analysis: Multiple goroutines send to kzgChan (buffered at 100). The kzgVerifierRoutine drains the channel and batches all pending entries, then calls verifyKzgBatch which is single-goroutine serialized. No data race on allDataColumns construction.

phase2.summary: Attempting to trigger out-of-bounds commitment_indices: A malicious P2P peer would need sidecar.Index >= numberOfColumns (128). This is caught by VerifyDataColumnSidecar at line 37, returning ErrIndexTooLarge and ValidationReject BEFORE the KZG path. No path exists where cellIndices exceeds numberOfColumns after passing ValidFields(). The C library enforces additional internal validation for cell_index values.
phase2.counterexample: No counterexample found for commitment_indices out-of-bounds via normal P2P path. The guard at VerifyDataColumnSidecar/ValidFields blocks sidecar.Index >= 128 before KZG verification.
attack_scenarios: Attacker sends DataColumnSidecar with sidecar.Index = 200 (> 127): BLOCKED by VerifyDataColumnSidecar line 37, returns ErrIndexTooLarge, ValidationReject.
Attacker sends sidecar.Index = 127 with valid KZG indices: passes through correctly, column index passed as uint64 to C library as intended.

Theoretical TOCTOU: If numberOfColumns config changes between ValidFields() and VerifyCellKZGProofBatch, an index valid at check time could be slightly out-of-range at use time. But this is a config read (not dynamic state), and the C library handles out-of-range cell indices with error returns, not crashes.

phase2_5.summary: The validateDataColumn function is registered as a libp2p pubsub validator, directly exposed to P2P gossip messages from any peer. The ValidFields() guard runs before KZG verification on every incoming message. The guard is placed correctly in the validation sequence per the Ethereum spec ordering.
phase2_5.reasoning: The out-of-bounds commitment_indices scenario as described is blocked by ValidFields() before KZG processing is reached.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'sidecar.Index < numberOfColumns at KZG verification time' holds. VerifyDataColumnSidecar enforces it synchronously before validateWithKzgBatchVerifier is called. The c-kzg-4844 binding independently validates equal array lengths. The Go wrapper VerifyCellKZGProofBatch does not add its own length check, but this is compensated by the construction logic in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs which builds equal-length arrays by design.
phase3.guard_identified: VerifyDataColumnSidecar (p2p_interface.go:37): sidecar.Index >= numberOfColumns returns ErrIndexTooLarge. c-kzg-4844 Go binding validates equal array lengths.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Guards are sufficient for the specific property of commitment_indices bounds. The check occurs prior to and independently of KZG verification. The C library binding provides a second layer.
edge_cases: numberOfColumns is read from params.BeaconConfig() at validation time - config fork could cause inconsistency, but not a memory safety issue.

The Go wrapper VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:98-106) does not validate lengths - it relies on the C binding. This is a defense-in-depth gap but not exploitable given equal-length array construction upstream.

phase3_5.reason: The property as stated (commitment_indices out-of-bounds causing memory safety violation) is not achievable. VerifyDataColumnSidecar validates the column index before KZG processing. The premise of the check item (commitment_indices as array indices into commitments) is a semantic misunderstanding - they are column identifiers (0-127), not array offsets.
phase3_5.recommendation: No code change required for this specific check. Documentation clarification: cellIndices in this codebase are column identifiers passed to the C library for polynomial evaluation, not array offsets into the commitments array.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Can a malicious P2P peer cause validator node crash by sending crafted commitment_indices exceeding array bounds?

phase1.summary: This check asks about crash-via-out-of-bounds from a P2P peer. The abstract state machine shows: (1) P2P message -> ValidFields() -> index range check -> if invalid: return Reject, no KZG call. (2) If ValidFields passes: sidecar.Index guaranteed < numberOfColumns. (3) KZG batch path: arrays built with equal lengths guaranteed by single-loop construction. (4) C library called with guaranteed-equal-length arrays and valid column indices. The abstract domain for sidecar.Index after ValidFields is [0, 127]. No OOB array access possible in Go; Go panics (not undefined behavior) on OOB. The C library returns C_KZG_BADARGS as error, not segfault.
state_anomalies: CRITICAL: The batch verifier (verifyKzgBatch, batch_verifier.go:194-214) mixes data columns from MULTIPLE P2P validators into a single verification call. A malicious peer injecting an invalid column will cause ALL pending legitimate verifiers to receive an error response simultaneously, triggering N individual re-verification calls. This is a CPU amplification DoS.

The kzgChan buffer is 100. Under heavy adversarial load, if a malicious peer floods the channel near capacity with invalid columns, legitimate messages may block on channel send (line 165), causing validation to hang until slot timeout, leading to ValidationIgnore instead of Accept.
Go arrays are bounds-checked. Even if sidecar.Index were passed as an array index (it is not), Go would panic with a recoverable panic, not memory corruption.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: kzgVerifierRoutine drains ALL pending kzgVerifier entries from the channel in a tight inner loop (lines 69-80) using default: case to stop draining when channel is empty. ALL collected entries are passed to verifyKzgBatch. If one entry fails, ALL get the same error, ALL fall back to individual verification. N malicious columns mixed with M legitimate ones causes M+N individual KZG verifications.

phase2.summary: No path exists for memory corruption or process crash via P2P message. The attacker can cause computational amplification: send invalid DataColumnSidecar messages timed to coincide with legitimate messages in the kzgChan queue. The batch verifier groups them together, fails the batch, and all N legitimate verifiers fall back to individual verification. This is a real DoS vector through CPU exhaustion, not memory safety.
phase2.counterexample: DoS amplification scenario: Attacker sends M invalid DataColumnSidecar messages (each passing ValidFields: valid index in range, non-zero commitments, matching column/commitment/proof lengths, but corrupted KZG proof bytes) timed to coincide with N legitimate verifiers in kzgChan. verifyKzgBatch collects all M+N, calls VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs once (batch), which fails due to attacker's M invalid proofs. All M+N verifiers receive the same error and fall back to validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg. Result: M+N individual KZG calls instead of 1 batch. KZG proof verification costs ~1-10ms each. For M=N=50 (half channel): 101 KZG calls instead of 1. ~100x amplification.
attack_scenarios: Batch pollution DoS: Send crafted DataColumnSidecars with valid structural fields (ValidFields passes: valid index, non-zero commitments, matching array lengths) but corrupted KZG proof data (flip one byte in KzgProofs). These pass all pre-KZG checks, enter kzgChan, get batched with legitimate traffic, corrupt the batch, force individual re-verification for all co-batched legitimate columns.

Channel saturation: Flood kzgChan (cap 100) with invalid columns from multiple peers, causing legitimate validators to block on the channel send at line 165 for up to slot_duration timeout, resulting in ValidationIgnore for legitimate columns (slot misses).
Timing amplification: Send invalid columns just before a legitimate block's columns arrive to maximize co-batching probability and CPU amplification.

phase2_5.summary: Any connected P2P peer can send DataColumnSidecar gossip messages. The kzgChan is shared across ALL incoming data column validators. A peer that crafts structurally valid (passes ValidFields) but cryptographically invalid (fails KZG) columns has a direct path to the batch verifier. The gossip scoring mechanism does score peers based on behavior, but KZG verification is expensive enough that significant damage can be done before sufficient score penalty accumulates to trigger peer disconnect.
entry_points: P2P gossip subscription for data_column_sidecar_N subnets (N=0..NUM_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECAR_SUBNETS-1)
phase2_5.reasoning: Any connected peer on any data column sidecar subnet can inject messages that pass structural validation but fail KZG verification. The batch grouping mechanism in kzgVerifierRoutine creates the amplification surface. No rate limiting is applied before the kzgChan enqueue.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'no P2P message can crash the validator node' holds - there is no memory safety violation, no panic path from valid-but-corrupted KZG data. The invariant 'P2P messages do not cause disproportionate computational load' does NOT hold. The batch verifier design of sending the same error to all co-batched verifiers, combined with the fallback to individual re-verification, creates a provable computational amplification vulnerability.
phase3.guard_identified: ValidFields() for structural validation. KZG batch verification with individual fallback for cryptographic validation. GossipScorer for peer reputation (eventual, not preventive).
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Guards are sufficient to prevent crashes and incorrect acceptance of invalid data. Guards are NOT sufficient to prevent DoS amplification via batch pollution. The fallback mechanism (validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg) is intended to handle transient batch failures but creates an amplification surface when combined with adversarial inputs that pass structural but fail cryptographic validation.
edge_cases: A single malicious peer with many connections (via different peer IDs) could multiply the attack surface proportionally.
Under high legitimate load, the kzgChan cap of 100 becomes a bottleneck; adding adversarial load could starve legitimate validators, causing slot misses.
The fallback path validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg is NOT rate-limited separately from the batch path.

phase3_5.reason: A real DoS amplification vector exists: adversarial P2P peers can cause disproportionate KZG verification work by poisoning shared batch verifier runs. The node will not crash (memory safety is preserved) but can be made to spend significantly more CPU on KZG verification than necessary (~100x amplification based on kzgChan buffer size of 100), potentially causing slot misses or degraded performance. This is reachable from any connected P2P peer without special privileges.
phase3_5.recommendation: 1. Per-source batch isolation: Group kzgVerifier entries by peer ID or trust level before batching. 2. Bisection fallback: After batch failure, use binary search to isolate the invalid subset rather than falling back individually for all. 3. Per-peer rate limiting before kzgChan enqueue. 4. Move seenDataColumnCache check before KZG verification to skip already-seen columns.
phase3_5.severity_estimate: Medium - DoS amplification from any connected P2P peer, causing up to ~100x KZG computation overhead, potential slot misses under sustained attack.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: What is the memory safety impact of out-of-bounds commitment_indices access in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl?

phase1.summary: Memory safety analysis of the Go-to-C-library boundary. In Go, all slice accesses are bounds-checked at runtime (recoverable panic on OOB, not undefined behavior). The C library (c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1) receives data via unsafe.Pointer casts from Go slices. The Go binding validates len(commitmentsBytes) == len(cells) == len(cellIndices) == len(proofsBytes) before calling C. The C function receives num_cells as the authoritative count and uses it to bound all array accesses. cellIndices contains column identifiers (0-127), not array offsets, so their magnitude does not cause memory access beyond the provided arrays.
state_anomalies: The Go wrapper VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:98-106) does NOT validate array lengths before calling the Go binding ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch. However, the Go binding itself validates at its entry point. The missing validation in the Go wrapper is a defense-in-depth gap but not an exploitable vulnerability given the binding-level check.

Arrays are passed to C via *(**C.Bytes48)(unsafe.Pointer(&commitmentsBytes)) - this takes the address of the slice header to get the backing array pointer. If all slices are empty (len=0), equal-length check passes (0==0) and C is called with num_cells=0. Behavior of C library with zero-length inputs and potentially nil pointers needs C-level verification.

The construction logic in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs (p2p_interface.go:73-80) uses 'for i := range sidecar.Column' with accesses to sidecar.KzgCommitments[i] and sidecar.KzgProofs[i]. ValidFields ensures len(Column)==len(KzgCommitments)==len(KzgProofs), so this is protected from OOB.
phase1.language_safety: Go: all slice accesses bounds-checked, OOB causes panic (recoverable), not memory corruption. C library (c-kzg-4844): validates inputs before access, returns C_KZG_BADARGS on invalid inputs. No memory corruption risk identified.

phase2.summary: Attempting to construct a memory safety exploit path via P2P input: All paths that reach the C library boundary have already been filtered by ValidFields() ensuring structural consistency and by the Go binding's length check. The only way to reach C with mismatched lengths would require bypassing both the Go-layer construction (which guarantees equal lengths by design) and the binding-level check (which explicitly validates). Neither bypass is achievable through P2P message content alone.
phase2.counterexample: No counterexample found. All P2P paths that reach VerifyCellKZGProofBatch have equal-length arrays guaranteed by: (1) VerifyDataColumnSidecar's mismatch check, (2) single-loop construction in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs, (3) c-kzg-4844 Go binding length check.
attack_scenarios: Hypothetical: Corrupt Go runtime to skip bounds checks - not in scope.

Hypothetical: Exploit a bug in c-kzg-4844 C library itself with valid-format but cryptographically crafted cell indices or commitment bytes - separate C library vulnerability outside this codebase's scope.

Hypothetical: Future code change removes ValidFields() call before KZG verification - equal-length constraint in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs could be violated if KzgCommitments, Column, and KzgProofs differ in length.

phase2_5.summary: The memory safety concern as stated requires reaching the C library with out-of-bounds indices or mismatched array lengths. This requires bypassing ValidFields(), the array-construction logic, and the Go binding validation. No P2P-reachable path bypasses all three.
entry_points: P2P gossip (blocked by ValidFields before KZG)
phase2_5.reasoning: Memory safety violation via P2P is not achievable with the current code structure. The layered validation provides sufficient protection.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'all arrays passed to VerifyCellKZGProofBatch have equal lengths and valid column indices' is proven to hold for the P2P path. Constructive proof: VerifyDataColumnSidecar establishes len(Column)==len(KzgCommitments)==len(KzgProofs) and Index < numberOfColumns. VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs builds arrays in a single synchronized loop. The c-kzg-4844 binding re-validates before calling C. Three independent guards all agree.
phase3.guard_identified: Three-layer defense: (1) VerifyDataColumnSidecar structural validation, (2) single-loop construction guaranteeing equal lengths by construction, (3) c-kzg-4844 Go binding explicit length check before C call.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Guards are sufficient and redundant for memory safety. The Go wrapper layer (kzg.go:98-106) missing its own length check is a defense-in-depth gap but not a vulnerability given the binding-level check.
edge_cases: If c-kzg-4844 C library itself has memory safety issues with valid-format but semantically crafted inputs, that is a separate C library vulnerability outside this codebase's scope.
The CGo pattern for empty slice pointers warrants verification in the c-kzg-4844 binding for zero-cell edge case.

phase3_5.reason: No memory safety violation is reachable via P2P inputs in the current code. The three independent guards collectively prevent out-of-bounds conditions from reaching the C library. The Go runtime's bounds checking ensures panic (not corruption) even if somehow an OOB access were attempted. The concern about the Go wrapper (kzg.go) missing its own length validation is a defense-in-depth observation but not an exploitable vulnerability.
phase3_5.recommendation: Add explicit length validation in VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go) as defense-in-depth. Document the invariant that all four input slices must have equal length. Consider adding a test specifically for the empty-slice CGo boundary behavior in c-kzg-4844 bindings.
phase3_5.severity_estimate: Low (informational - not an exploitable memory safety issue)

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002: Are all four input arrays (commitment_bytes, cell_indices, cells, proofs_bytes) validated for equal length in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch?

phase1.summary: Analyzing the length validation state across the call chain. The Go wrapper VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:98-106) does NOT explicitly validate equal lengths of its four inputs. It converts Cell types and delegates to ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch. The ckzg4844 Go binding validates: 'if len(commitmentsBytes) != len(cells) || len(cellIndices) != len(cells) || len(proofsBytes) != len(cells)'. The validation exists at the binding layer, not the Go wrapper layer. For P2P paths, the construction logic in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs guarantees equal lengths by building all four arrays in a single synchronized loop.
state_anomalies: The Go wrapper VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:98-106) is a public function that can be called from anywhere with arbitrary slice lengths. Any caller that bypasses VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs could pass mismatched lengths. The binding-level check would return ErrBadArgs, not crash.
The property asks specifically about verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch (kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch). This function at lines 98-106 has no length validation. It relies on the caller and the binding.
If empty slices (len=0 for all) are passed, the binding check passes (0==0). C call proceeds with num_cells=0. C library behavior with zero-length inputs needs verification.
phase1.validation_layer_analysis: P2P layer: VerifyDataColumnSidecar validates per-sidecar consistency (len(Column)==len(KzgCommitments)==len(KzgProofs)). Array-building layer: single-loop construction in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs guarantees equal-length by construction. C boundary layer: c-kzg-4844 Go binding validates equal lengths explicitly. The Go wrapper layer (kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch) is the only layer lacking explicit validation.

phase2.summary: Attempting to trigger a vulnerability via mismatched lengths. Direct P2P path: guaranteed equal by construction before reaching VerifyCellKZGProofBatch. Direct API call (hypothetical): kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch called with len(commitments)=5, len(cellIndices)=3, len(cells)=5, len(proofs)=5. Result: ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch returns (false, ErrBadArgs). This is handled gracefully. No crash.
phase2.counterexample: No exploitable counterexample for equal-length validation failure. The binding-level check is sufficient to prevent C-level memory safety issues.
attack_scenarios: Internal caller (non-P2P) provides mismatched arrays to kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch: Returns ErrBadArgs, handled gracefully. Not a vulnerability, but indicates the Go wrapper does not enforce the precondition it implicitly assumes.
Future code change adds a new call site with user-controlled arrays bypassing VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs: Would fail at binding level with ErrBadArgs.

phase2_5.summary: The length mismatch concern at the Go wrapper level is only reachable from internal Go code, not from P2P inputs directly. P2P inputs are processed through VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs which guarantees equal-length arrays before calling kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch. Any internal call with mismatched lengths gets ErrBadArgs from the binding.
entry_points: Internal Go code calling kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch directly
phase2_5.reasoning: No P2P-reachable attack surface for length mismatch. The construction in VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs is the single P2P-originating path to this function, and it guarantees equal lengths.

phase3.summary: The invariant 'all four arrays have equal length at the C call boundary' holds. It is enforced by the c-kzg-4844 Go binding. The Go wrapper (kzg.go:98-106) does not itself validate, relying on callers and the binding. The P2P path (VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs) provides an additional constructive guarantee. The invariant is upheld but the guard is one layer lower than ideal from a defensive programming standpoint.
phase3.guard_identified: c-kzg-4844 Go binding: if len(commitmentsBytes) != len(cells) || len(cellIndices) != len(cells) || len(proofsBytes) != len(cells) { return false, ErrBadArgs }. Also: VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs single-loop construction.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for safety. The absence of the check in the Go wrapper is a code quality concern, not a security vulnerability. However, if the c-kzg-4844 library binding changes or is replaced, the wrapper's lack of validation would become a direct security issue.
edge_cases: Empty input (all length 0): binding check passes (0==0), C called with num_cells=0. C library behavior with zero cells warrants verification.
If the c-kzg-4844 library is replaced and the binding-level check is removed, the Go wrapper's lack of validation would become a security issue.

phase3_5.reason: The equal-length validation is present in the c-kzg-4844 Go binding. For all P2P-reachable paths, the construction logic additionally guarantees equal lengths by design. The missing check in the Go wrapper (kzg.go) is a defense-in-depth and code quality concern, not an exploitable vulnerability.
phase3_5.recommendation: Add explicit length validation in VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go) as defense-in-depth: 'if len(commitmentsBytes) != len(cellIndices) || len(cellIndices) != len(cells) || len(cells) != len(proofsBytes) { return false, errors.New("mismatched input lengths") }'. This makes the precondition explicit at the Go wrapper layer and provides protection if the C binding changes.
phase3_5.severity_estimate: Low (defense-in-depth recommendation, not an exploitable vulnerability)

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Does P2P gossip validation enforce equal-length constraint on batch KZG proof verification inputs before reaching verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch?

phase1.summary: Full analysis of the P2P path to verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch. Validation chain: (1) decodePubsubMessage - proto decode, structural integrity. (2) ValidFields() -> VerifyDataColumnSidecar: enforces len(Column)==len(KzgCommitments)==len(KzgProofs) and 0 < len. (3) validateWithKzgBatchVerifier -> verifyKzgBatch -> VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs: builds arrays in synchronized single-loop. (4) kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch: no own validation. (5) ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch: validates equal length. The equal-length constraint is enforced at steps 2 and 5.
state_anomalies: CRITICAL: The batch verifier batches data from MULTIPLE P2P validators (verifyKzgBatch, batch_verifier.go:194-214). While each individual DataColumnSidecar has guaranteed equal-length arrays after ValidFields, the batch construction concatenates arrays from multiple sidecars. The concatenated arrays are still equal-length because each sidecar contributes equally to all four arrays per the synchronized loop - but this is correct by construction only.

The fallback path (validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg) is triggered when verifyKzgBatch fails. The fallback calls VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs again with each individual validator's dataColumns slice. Individual sidecars have been validated by ValidFields, so equal-length holds for the fallback path too.

CRITICAL DoS: The seenDataColumnCache check (line 157, validate_data_column.go) occurs AFTER KZG verification. An attacker can send the same invalid column repeatedly (from different peer IDs), forcing repeated full validation including KZG batch grouping before the seen-check would reject it.
phase1.concurrency_analysis: The kzgVerifierRoutine is the single KZG bottleneck. It processes all pending KZG verifications serially in batches. Under high load, multiple goroutines sending to kzgChan compete for the 100-slot buffer. The fallback from batch failure spawns additional VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs calls in message-handling goroutines, shifting CPU load to those goroutines.

phase2.summary: Complete attack scenario exploiting batch verifier pollution: Attack: Peer A sends 100 valid DataColumnSidecar messages (legitimate blocks). Peer B (attacker) sends 100 structurally-valid-but-KZG-invalid DataColumnSidecar messages simultaneously. kzgVerifierRoutine drains all 200 kzgVerifier entries in one burst. verifyKzgBatch is called with combined allDataColumns of 200 sidecars. Batch fails due to attacker's invalid proofs. ALL 200 kzgVerifier.resChan receive the same error. All 200 validators fall back to validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg. Peer A's valid messages: 100 individual verifications, each succeeds. Peer B's invalid: 100 individual verifications, each fails. Total KZG verifications: 1 (batch, failed) + 200 (individual) = 201 instead of 1 optimistic. CPU amplification: ~201x.
phase2.counterexample: Batch DoS amplification: Attacker sends N invalid messages (structurally valid: valid index < 128, non-zero commitments, matching Column/KzgCommitments/KzgProofs lengths, but corrupted KZG proof bytes) coinciding with M legitimate messages in kzgChan. verifyKzgBatch processes N+M together, fails, forces N+M individual KZG verifications. CPU cost: 1 batch + (N+M) individual verifications = N+M+1 instead of 1 (all valid) or N+M (pessimistic). For N=M=50 (half channel): 101 verifications instead of 1. Amplification: ~100x.
attack_scenarios: Batch pollution via structurally valid, KZG invalid messages: Passes all pre-KZG checks (ValidFields, subnet, slot, parent, proposer signature), enters batch verifier, poisons the batch, forces individual fallback for all co-batched messages. Most effective attack.

Channel saturation: Fill kzgChan (cap=100) with invalid messages before legitimate column sidecars arrive. Legitimate message blocks on channel send at line 165 for up to slot_duration seconds. If slot_duration expires, ValidationIgnore returned for legitimate column - slot miss.

Gossip scoring bypass: The gossip scorer penalizes peers for invalid messages, but the scoring is applied after damage is done and requires accumulated evidence before peer disconnect. Attacker can rotate peer IDs to avoid sustained score penalty.

phase2_5.summary: The equal-length constraint itself is enforced before verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch (question answered: yes). But the adversarial analysis reveals a more significant finding: the design of verifyKzgBatch creates a CPU amplification DoS vector that is fully P2P-reachable. Any connected peer on any data column subnet can exploit this by sending structurally valid but cryptographically invalid messages timed to coincide with legitimate traffic.
entry_points: P2P gossip on any data_column_sidecar_N topic (N=0..NUM_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECAR_SUBNETS-1)
Direct libp2p connection followed by topic subscription and message publication
phase2_5.reasoning: The attack surface is the kzgChan shared by all incoming data column validators. Any peer that can send gossip messages (all connected peers) can inject into the kzgChan. The batch pollution attack does not require any special privileges or Sybil attack - a single malicious peer is sufficient to cause amplification.

phase3.summary: Invariant 1 (equal-length before verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch): HOLDS. Enforced by VerifyDataColumnSidecar and synchronized loop construction. Invariant 2 (KZG verification cost bounded by number of received messages): DOES NOT HOLD. The fallback mechanism creates O(N) total KZG verification work for N received messages (instead of O(1) batch), even when only a small fraction are invalid. In the worst case (1 invalid mixed with kzgChan capacity of 100 legitimate), the amplification factor is 100x.
phase3.guard_identified: Equal-length guards: VerifyDataColumnSidecar + c-kzg-4844 binding (sufficient). DoS amplification guards: none - the gossip scorer provides eventual remediation but not prevention.
phase3.guard_sufficiency: Guards for equal-length are sufficient. Guards for DoS amplification are absent. The design choice to send the same error to ALL co-batched verifiers when the batch fails is the root cause of the vulnerability.
edge_cases: Empty batch (len(kzgBatch)==0): verifyKzgBatch returns early at line 195-197. Correct.
Single-element batch: No amplification, direct 1:1 verification.
Full channel (100 entries, all invalid): 100 individual fallback verifications + 1 batch = 101 KZG calls instead of 1.

Context cancellation timing: If the batch verification itself consumes most of the slot timeout, the fallback may have very little time remaining, causing validation to time out and return ValidationIgnore even for valid columns.

phase3_5.reason: Two distinct issues found: (1) The equal-length validation question is answered YES (enforced before verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch). (2) A real, exploitable DoS amplification vulnerability exists in the batch verifier design: malicious P2P peers can cause up to ~100x KZG computation overhead (based on kzgChan buffer size) by poisoning batch verification runs with structurally-valid-but-KZG-invalid messages. Reachable from any connected P2P peer with no special privileges. Node will not crash but can suffer performance degradation leading to missed slots or delayed validation of legitimate data columns. This is a medium-severity DoS vulnerability.
phase3_5.recommendation: 1. Per-source batch isolation in verifyKzgBatch: Group kzgVerifier entries by peer ID to prevent cross-peer batch poisoning. 2. Bisection fallback: After batch failure, use binary search to isolate the invalid subset, allowing valid subset to be verified normally without full individual fallback for all. 3. Per-peer rate limiting before kzgChan enqueue. 4. Move seenDataColumnCache check before KZG verification to avoid redundant KZG work for already-rejected (slot, proposer, index) tuples. 5. Consider bounding kzgChan draining per cycle to limit maximum amplification.
phase3_5.severity_estimate: Medium - exploitable DoS amplification from any connected P2P peer, causing up to ~100x KZG computation overhead per batch cycle, potential slot misses under sustained attack.
